name: Pelican
lede: Pelican is a dark, nearly neutral grey from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color, and no book we hold says why it carries a bird's name.

sections.title: A name without a story
sections.body:
Pelican comes from Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* of 1930, where it sits on plate 47 and was first recorded in 1925 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it as "dark gray", 3.8 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale, and its chroma is only about 3, so it is close to a true neutral with a faint yellow-green cast [1]. Why the authors chose the bird's name is undocumented [1].

The books in our collection use "pelican" for other things entirely. The ship in which Francis Drake sailed around the world in 1577, later renamed the Golden Hind, was the *Pelican*, and Drake carried hopes of cochineal on board [2]. Alchemists used a glass retort called a pelican [3][4]. Ball mentions monastral blue, familiar from the covers of old Pelican books, a synthetic blue with a copper ion at its center, which is not this grey [5].

sections.title: Neighbors
sections.body: The swatch is a near neighbor of [[battleship-grey]] and [[bluish-grey]], and in our archive it appears on the same canvases as those two more often than chance [6]. It also sits close to [[grey]] itself, but darker and slightly greener than a mid-grey. None of this makes it a plumage color: no book describes a pelican's feathers in these terms.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a common color on canvas. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 905 works, or 3.81 per cent, which is more common than 83 per cent of the named colors [6]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 4.1 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from then (68 paintings) [6]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone [6]. The most devoted painter is Arnoud van Halen, with it in 10 of 50 works [6].

It shares canvases with Battleship Grey (lift 9.7, n=63) and Bluish Grey (lift 5.5, n=51) [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, where whites and blacks both drift toward grey, so many of these matches are a color the painter did not choose [6].
